headline: Massachusetts protects 580 acres in Blandford wildlife corridor
dek: The new public conservation land links more than 39,000 acres across the Mass. Pike while adding habitat and outdoor recreation space in western Massachusetts.
body: Massachusetts conservation agencies and The Nature Conservancy have completed a project protecting more than 580 acres in Blandford, creating new public land on both sides of Interstate 90 and strengthening a wildlife connection through the western Massachusetts hills. The [Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-protects-over-580-acres-for-wildlife-and-outdoor-recreation-in-blandford) announced the project Oct. 2. [Western Mass News](https://www.westernmassnews.com/2026/10/03/more-land-added-chester-blandford-stare-forest/) independently reported the same acreage and the new designations.

The protected property is divided into a 360-acre MassWildlife Blandford Wildlife Management Area and a 218-acre addition to Chester-Blandford State Forest. The former Christmas tree farm crosses the Mass. Pike and connects more than 39,000 acres of already protected land, according to state officials and the local report. That makes the project more than a stand-alone open-space purchase: it closes a gap in a larger landscape where animals can move between habitat on opposite sides of one of New England's busiest highways.

The land is open to the public for outdoor recreation, although the announcement did not provide a separate trail map, parking plan or operating schedule for the new management area. Residents and visitors will need to rely on updates from MassWildlife and the Department of Conservation and Recreation for practical access information as management details are posted.

The property contains mature and young forest, agricultural grasslands, wetlands and four brooks: Sanderson, Cushman, Finley and Peebles. Those waterways are part of the Westfield River watershed. State agencies said the conservation work will help protect water quality and nearby drinking-water supplies, while preserving cold-water fish habitat used by species such as Eastern brook trout.

The corridor also has a direct transportation-safety dimension. The state says MassWildlife, DCR, MassDOT and the Nature Conservancy have been working to understand how animals cross roads and highways. At the Blandford site, MassDOT and the Nature Conservancy are monitoring a culvert under I-90, where black bears, bobcats, coyotes, river otters and other wildlife have been documented passing through, according to the state announcement. Keeping that route connected can help animals reach food, water and seasonal habitat while giving planners evidence for future crossing improvements.

The project includes habitat that can support the New England cottontail, Massachusetts' only native rabbit, which state officials describe as vulnerable to habitat loss. Protecting connected forest and grassland does not guarantee that the rabbit or any other species will expand here, but it preserves the kind of varied landscape wildlife managers say is necessary for movement and adaptation as conditions change.

Blandford's acquisition is part of a broader state conservation strategy. Massachusetts' Biodiversity Goals call for doubling the pace of land and water protection, with targets of conserving 30 percent by 2030 and 40 percent by 2050. The administration said its proposed Mass Ready Act includes $304.5 million for land-protection programs and $20 million tied to biodiversity goals; those are proposed investments, not funds this project alone received.

For the Hilltowns, the immediate result is a permanently protected stretch of forest, streams and open land that can serve both residents and wildlife. The agencies involved still have to translate the acquisition into day-to-day public access and long-term habitat management. The new designations give them the protected footprint; future agency plans will determine how visitors use it and how the corridor is monitored over time.
